title: Annihilation of Caste
author: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar
tts_script: You are standing before Annihilation of Caste, written by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar in 1936. It began as a speech he was never allowed to give. The organisers read the text, asked him to soften it, and cancelled their own conference when he refused to change a single comma. He printed fifteen hundred copies himself, and it has not been out of print since.
full_content: Overview: Annihilation of Caste is Dr. B.R. Ambedkar's best known work of social criticism, published on 15 May 1936. Historical context: The Jat-Pat Todak Mandal, a Hindu reformist society in Lahore, invited Ambedkar in a letter dated 12 December 1935 to address their 1936 annual conference on the caste system. When the organisers read the prepared text they found its criticism of Hindu scripture and its argument for religious conversion unacceptable, and asked him to remove passages. Ambedkar replied that he would not change a comma. The Mandal cancelled the conference rather than host the speech. Key facts: Ambedkar self published 1,500 copies at his own expense on 15 May 1936, after the Mandal declined to print it. Mahatma Gandhi responded in July 1936 in his weekly Harijan with an article titled A Vindication of Caste, and Ambedkar's rebuttal was bound into the second edition of 1937, retitled Annihilation of Caste: With a Reply to Mahatma Gandhi. Significance: The central argument is that caste cannot be reformed away by inter-caste dining or inter-caste marriage alone, because caste rests on religious sanction. As Ambedkar put it, the enemy you must grapple with is not the people who observe caste, but the Shastras that teach it. Notable details: A widely read annotated edition was published by Navayana in 2014 with an introduction by Arundhati Roy titled The Doctor and the Saint. The text remains among the most cited works in Indian social thought.

title: The Buddha and His Dhamma
author: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar
tts_script: This is The Buddha and His Dhamma, the last work Dr. Ambedkar completed. He finished the manuscript in 1956, weeks before his death, and never saw it in print, because he could not afford to publish it in his lifetime. It appeared in 1957, and became the founding text for the millions who followed him into Buddhism.
full_content: Overview: The Buddha and His Dhamma is Dr. B.R. Ambedkar's final book and the founding text of the Buddhist movement he began in India. Historical context: Ambedkar worked on the manuscript for roughly five years. He completed it in 1956, the same year he formally converted to Buddhism at Nagpur on 14 October. He died on 6 December 1956, and the book was published posthumously in 1957, because he had not been able to raise the money to print it during his lifetime. Key facts: The book retells the life of the Buddha and presents the Dhamma as a social and ethical system rather than a set of metaphysical claims. Ambedkar reorganises the traditional material, setting aside doctrines he regarded as later additions, and foregrounding the Buddha's teaching on suffering, equality and moral responsibility between people. Significance: It gave the new Buddhist converts of 1956 and after a text of their own, and it is read at Buddhist gatherings across Maharashtra to this day. The tradition it began is often called Navayana, meaning the new vehicle. Notable details: Alongside the Three Jewels and the Five Precepts, Ambedkar composed 22 vows for converts which set out a decisive break with the caste order. Copies of this book are sold in enormous numbers at Deekshabhoomi each year on Dhammachakra Pravartan Din.

title: The Constitution of India
author: Drafting Committee, chaired by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar
tts_script: Before you is the Constitution of India. Dr. Ambedkar chaired the seven member Drafting Committee from August 1947, and the Assembly adopted the text on the twenty sixth of November 1949. It took two years, eleven months and eighteen days to write. Article seventeen abolished untouchability outright, the practice that had shaped his own childhood.
full_content: Overview: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar was elected Chairman of the Drafting Committee of the Constituent Assembly of India on 29 August 1947, and piloted the drafting of the Constitution through the Assembly. Historical context: The Committee had seven members. The Assembly debated and revised the draft over 2 years, 11 months and 18 days. It adopted the Constitution on 26 November 1949, now marked as Constitution Day, and the document came into force on 26 January 1950, which India observes as Republic Day. As adopted it ran to 395 Articles, 22 Parts and 8 Schedules. Key facts: Article 17 abolishes untouchability and forbids its practice in any form. Article 32 guarantees the right to move the Supreme Court directly when a fundamental right is violated. Speaking in the Assembly on 9 December 1948, Ambedkar said that if he were asked to name the single most important article, an article without which the Constitution would be a nullity, he could point to no other than this one, calling it the very soul of the Constitution and the very heart of it. Significance: For a man born into a community denied the use of public wells and public schools, drafting the guarantee of equal citizenship was the work of a lifetime. Notable details: Ambedkar served as independent India's first Law Minister from 15 August 1947. He resigned on 6 October 1951 after the Hindu Code Bill, his attempt to reform personal law on marriage, divorce and inheritance, was blocked in Parliament.

title: Deekshabhoomi, Nagpur
author: Sheo Dan Mal, architect
tts_script: This is Deekshabhoomi in Nagpur, the ground where Dr. Ambedkar became a Buddhist on the fourteenth of October 1956. Around four hundred thousand people converted alongside him that day. The great white stupa that now stands here took more than twenty years to build, and is the largest hollow stupa in the world.
full_content: Overview: Deekshabhoomi in Nagpur, Maharashtra, is the site where Dr. B.R. Ambedkar embraced Buddhism, and the most visited of the memorials associated with him. Historical context: On 14 October 1956 the Burmese monk Bhadant Mahasthavir Chandramani administered the Three Jewels and the Five Precepts to Ambedkar and his wife Savita. Ambedkar then administered the same, together with 22 vows of his own composition, to the crowd that had gathered. Roughly 400,000 followers, most of them Dalits, converted that day in a single ceremony. The conversions continued after his death and ran into the millions by March 1959. Key facts: Construction of the stupa began in July 1978 and it was inaugurated on 18 December 2001 by the President of India, K. R. Narayanan. The architect was Sheo Dan Mal, who modelled it on the great stupa at Sanchi. Its ground floor holds a square hall measuring 211 feet on each side, and it is described as the largest hollow stupa among all Buddhist stupas in the world. Significance: Deekshabhoomi is one of the five Panchteerth sites designated by the Government of India. Notable details: Every year on Dhammachakra Pravartan Din, marking the anniversary of the conversion, hundreds of thousands of pilgrims gather here, and books worth crores of rupees are sold in a single day.

title: Chaitya Bhoomi, Mumbai
author: Memorial to Dr. B.R. Ambedkar
tts_script: This is Chaitya Bhoomi at Dadar in Mumbai, beside the sea, where Dr. Ambedkar was cremated on the seventh of December 1956. Half a million mourners came. The chaitya raised over the spot opened in 1971. Its gateway is a replica of the great gate at Sanchi, and an Ashoka pillar stands inside.
full_content: Overview: Chaitya Bhoomi, at Dadar in Mumbai beside Dadar Chowpatty beach, is the cremation place of Dr. B.R. Ambedkar and a Buddhist chaitya. Historical context: Ambedkar died at his Delhi residence on 6 December 1956, weeks after the conversion ceremony at Nagpur. His body was brought to Bombay and cremated on 7 December at Dadar Chowpatty, before a crowd estimated at half a million grieving people. Key facts: The stupa built over the site was opened on 5 December 1971. The structure is square in plan with a small dome, divided into a ground floor and a mezzanine. Its main entrance gate is a replica of the gateway of the Great Stupa at Sanchi, and a replica of the Ashoka Pillar stands inside. Significance: Chaitya Bhoomi is one of the five Panchteerth sites designated by the Government of India, alongside his birthplace at Mhow, his student lodgings in London, Deekshabhoomi at Nagpur, and the house at 26 Alipur Road in Delhi where he died. Notable details: Every year on 6 December, observed as Mahaparinirvan Din, very large crowds travel to Dadar to pay their respects. The surrounding streets fill with book stalls, and the day has become one of the largest gatherings in the city's calendar.

title: The Problem of the Rupee
author: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar
tts_script: The Problem of the Rupee was Dr. Ambedkar's doctoral thesis at the London School of Economics, published as a book in 1923. It examined why the rupee kept losing its value. Every member of the royal commission that went on to design India's central bank carried a copy of it.
full_content: Overview: The Problem of the Rupee: Its Origin and Its Solution is Dr. B.R. Ambedkar's study of Indian currency, submitted as his doctoral thesis at the London School of Economics under Professor Edwin Cannan and published in book form in 1923. Historical context: Ambedkar had already taken an MA at Columbia in 1915 and an MSc at the London School of Economics in 1921. The DSc awarded for this work in 1923 made him one of the most highly qualified economists in India at the time. Key facts: The book runs to some 257 pages and analyses the causes of the rupee's falling value, arguing for a currency standard that would hold prices stable rather than merely fix an exchange rate. When the Royal Commission on Indian Currency and Finance, known as the Hilton Young Commission, came to India, each of its members carried a copy, and Ambedkar gave evidence before it in 1926. Significance: The Commission's recommendations led to the Reserve Bank of India Act of 1934, and the Reserve Bank opened on 1 April 1935. Notable details: Ambedkar is remembered far more for his constitutional and social work than for his economics, but he trained as an economist first, and the currency question was the subject of his earliest sustained research.

title: Mooknayak and Bahishkrit Bharat
author: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, founder and editor
tts_script: Dr. Ambedkar was a newspaperman before he was a legislator. He launched Mooknayak, meaning Leader of the Silent, in 1920, and Bahishkrit Bharat, meaning Excluded India, in 1927. They gave a press to communities that no existing newspaper would report on fairly.
full_content: Overview: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar founded and edited a succession of Marathi periodicals, beginning with Mooknayak in 1920. Historical context: The mainstream Marathi press of the time either ignored the conditions of untouchable communities or reported them through the eyes of caste Hindu reformers. Ambedkar's answer was to publish his own papers. Mooknayak, whose name means Leader of the Silent, began as a fortnightly in 1920 with early support from Shahu Maharaj of Kolhapur. Bahishkrit Bharat, meaning Excluded India, followed in 1927, and later titles included Janata and Prabuddha Bharat. Key facts: These papers carried the arguments that later became his books and his speeches, on temple entry, on water rights, on separate electorates, and on the case for conversion. Significance: Journalism gave the movement a memory. Campaigns such as the Mahad Satyagraha of 1927 were organised, reported and defended in these pages. Notable details: Ambedkar wrote in Marathi for these audiences and in English for the colonial administration and the academy, and he moved between the two registers throughout his life.

title: The Mahad Satyagraha
author: Led by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar
tts_script: On the twentieth of March 1927, Dr. Ambedkar led thousands of people to the Chavdar tank at Mahad and drank from it. The water was public by law and forbidden by custom. It was the first mass action of his career, and it turned a legal right into a claim people were willing to march for.
full_content: Overview: The Mahad Satyagraha, also called the Chavdar Tale Satyagraha, was a mass action led by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar on 20 March 1927 to establish the right of untouchables to draw water from a public tank at Mahad, in what is now the Raigad district of Maharashtra. Historical context: The Bombay Legislative Council had passed a resolution opening public watering places to all communities, but custom continued to bar untouchable communities from the Chavdar tank. Ambedkar convened a conference at Mahad and, at its close, led the delegates to the tank to drink from it. Key facts: The action was met with violence, and the tank was ritually purified afterwards. A court case over access followed and ran for years. Significance: Mahad marked a change of method. Ambedkar had until then worked mainly through petitions, evidence to commissions and journalism. From 1927 onward he also used the organised mass assertion of rights. Notable details: At a second Mahad conference in December 1927 he publicly burned a copy of the Manusmriti, the text he held responsible for the religious sanction behind caste. The date is still observed in Maharashtra.

title: The Poona Pact
author: Agreement between Dr. B.R. Ambedkar and the representatives of M.K. Gandhi
tts_script: The Poona Pact was signed on the twenty fifth of September 1932. Gandhi had begun a fast to the death against separate electorates for the depressed classes. Ambedkar gave up the separate electorates and took reserved seats instead. Their number rose from seventy one to a hundred and forty eight.
full_content: Overview: The Poona Pact is the agreement signed on 25 September 1932 between Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, representing the depressed classes, and leaders acting for Mahatma Gandhi. Historical context: At the Round Table Conferences in London, Ambedkar argued for separate electorates for the depressed classes, so that their representatives would be chosen by their own voters rather than by a caste Hindu majority. The British Communal Award of 1932 granted this. Gandhi, imprisoned in Yerwada jail in Poona, began a fast unto death against it, holding that separate electorates would divide Hindu society permanently. Key facts: Under intense public pressure as Gandhi's condition worsened, Ambedkar agreed to give up separate electorates in exchange for seats reserved for the depressed classes within the general electorate. The number of reserved seats in the provincial legislatures rose from 71 under the Communal Award to 148 under the Pact. Significance: The reservation of seats established by the Pact was carried forward into the Constitution and shapes Indian electoral politics to this day. Notable details: Ambedkar regarded the circumstances of the agreement as coercive and wrote about it critically for the rest of his life, while accepting the settlement itself.

title: Columbia, the LSE and Gray's Inn
author: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar
tts_script: Dr. Ambedkar took a master's degree at Columbia in 1915, a master's at the London School of Economics in 1921, a doctorate of science there in 1923, and was called to the Bar at Gray's Inn the same year. Columbia awarded him a doctorate in 1927. He was among the most educated Indians of his generation.
full_content: Overview: Between 1913 and 1927 Dr. B.R. Ambedkar accumulated a set of qualifications almost unmatched in India at the time, across two continents and three institutions. Historical context: He graduated from Bombay University in 1912 with a BA in economics and political science. In 1913 Sayajirao Gaekwad, the Maharaja of Baroda, awarded him a scholarship to study at Columbia University in New York, on condition of later service to the state. Key facts: He took his MA at Columbia in June 1915, and presented the paper Castes in India: Their Mechanism, Genesis and Development at a seminar there in 1916. He enrolled at the London School of Economics and at Gray's Inn, but had to return to India in 1917 when his funding ended. He resumed his studies in London and completed an MSc in 1921 and a DSc in 1923, and was called to the Bar by Gray's Inn in 1923. Columbia awarded him the PhD in economics in 1927. Significance: The degrees mattered politically as well as intellectually. They made it impossible to dismiss his arguments on grounds of standing, in a society organised to deny him standing. Notable details: A house he lodged in at 10 King Henry's Road in London was bought by the Government of Maharashtra and opened as a memorial, Shiksha Bhoomi, in November 2015.

title: Rajgruha and the fifty thousand book library
author: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar's residence, Dadar, Mumbai
tts_script: Rajgruha in Dadar was Dr. Ambedkar's home, and he built it in large part to hold his books. His personal library grew past fifty thousand volumes, gathered across three continents. It was one of the largest private collections anyone has assembled.
full_content: Overview: Rajgruha is the house Dr. B.R. Ambedkar built in the Hindu Colony at Dadar in Mumbai in the early 1930s, and the home of his personal library. Historical context: Dadar was then developing as a planned residential district beyond the older core of the city. Ambedkar designed the house around his collection. The ground floor served as living space, while the upper floor was given over almost entirely to study and to shelving. Key facts: The library eventually held more than 50,000 books, collected over decades in Bombay, New York and London. It is often described as one of the largest personal libraries in the world. Significance: The collection was the working material behind his books, his evidence to commissions and his drafting work. A man barred as a child from drinking at the school water pot assembled a research library that few universities in India could match. Notable details: Rajgruha still stands and remains a place of pilgrimage for visitors, who come to see the house itself rather than a museum reconstruction of it.

title: The Hindu Code Bill and his resignation
author: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, first Law Minister of India
tts_script: Dr. Ambedkar was independent India's first Law Minister. His Hindu Code Bill would have given women the right to divorce and the right to inherit property. Parliament blocked it, and on the sixth of October 1951 he resigned over it.
full_content: Overview: The Hindu Code Bill was Dr. B.R. Ambedkar's attempt, as independent India's first Law Minister, to reform Hindu personal law, and its defeat was the reason he left the government. Historical context: Ambedkar took office as Law Minister on 15 August 1947. Alongside the drafting of the Constitution he prepared a comprehensive bill to codify Hindu personal law on marriage, divorce, adoption, guardianship and succession. Key facts: The bill proposed to give women the right to divorce and the right to inherit property, and to remove caste restrictions on marriage. It met sustained opposition inside and outside Parliament from those who saw it as an intrusion into religious law. It was cut down, delayed, and finally not passed in the form he had drafted. Ambedkar resigned on 6 October 1951. Significance: Much of the bill's substance was enacted in stages between 1955 and 1956 as four separate acts, after he had left office. Notable details: Ambedkar treated the equality of women as inseparable from the wider argument against caste, and regarded the bill's defeat as a more serious loss than any of the political reverses of his career.

title: The Bharat Ratna and the Panchteerth
author: Government of India
tts_script: India awarded Dr. Ambedkar the Bharat Ratna, its highest civilian honour, in 1990, thirty four years after his death. The government has since designated five sites connected with his life as the Panchteerth, from his birthplace at Mhow to the chaitya at Dadar.
full_content: Overview: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar was awarded the Bharat Ratna, India's highest civilian honour, in 1990, posthumously. Historical context: He died in 1956 having spent much of his political life in opposition to the governing party, and formal national recognition came slowly. The award in 1990, during the centenary period of his birth, marked a shift in how the Indian state described his place in its history. Key facts: The Government of India has designated five sites connected with his life as the Panchteerth, meaning the five pilgrimages. They are Janma Bhoomi at Mhow in Madhya Pradesh, where he was born on 14 April 1891; Shiksha Bhoomi in London, where he lodged while studying at the London School of Economics; Deeksha Bhoomi at Nagpur, where he converted to Buddhism on 14 October 1956; Mahaparinirvan Bhoomi at 26 Alipur Road in Delhi, where he died on 6 December 1956; and Chaitya Bhoomi at Dadar in Mumbai, where he was cremated. Significance: The memorial at Mhow was inaugurated on 14 April 1991, his hundredth birth anniversary. Notable details: His birthday, 14 April, is observed as Ambedkar Jayanti across India and is a public holiday in many states.
